title: A Critical Review of the Story of the Ramayana and an Account of South Indian Castes
author: V. P. Subramania Mudaliar
text: A Critical Review of THE STORY OF THE RAMAYANA AND AN ACCOUNT OF SOUTH INDIAN CASTES* BY MR. V. P. SUBRAMANIA MUDALIAR, G. B. V. C. INTRODUCTORY REMARKS. The late lamented Prof. P. Sundaram Pillai, M.A., Philosophy Professor, the Trivandram College, and the author of such rare works as 'மனேன் மணீயம்' and 'திற்கிறானை விளக்கம்' evinced much interest in historical researches. His "Milestones in the History of Tamil Literature" † is a standing monument to his work in that field. Certain truths brought to light in his researches, he did not kive to publish. His unpublished convictions on various subjects of importance are likely to be met with in his diaries, in his letters, or are engraved in the memory of those who had the fortune to converse with him on such topics. One evening in Madras, a few years before his death, he held a conversazione at which I was present. The subject of the conversation turning upon the Ramayana , one of his friends asked him for his views on the same. The views he expressed then form the basis of the present paper on the Ramayana . I do not possess either his impressive method of * This paper is a free translation of the "இராமாயண உள்ளுறை பொருள்" which appeared in No. 2, of the Tamilian Antiquary. † Vide The Tamilian Antiquary, No. 3. conveying conviction to his readers or the necessary historical training. It would have been much better if Mr. Sundaram Pillai had lived to publish his views on the subject. I expected that some of his friends better acquainted with him than myself would publish these views. As no such friend is forthcoming, I have to publish them for fear that they might otherwise be lost to the world. It is needless to add that any criticism of these views will have to be met by archaeologists who have made a study of the subject. Myself am an amateur and lay no claim to originality. The preface and the following pages are written as if they were Mr. Sundaram Pillai's. PREFACE. There are certain points which I should make clear to my readers before I publish my views on the Ramayana. I may without any vanity be allowed to say that I am behind few of my countrymen in point of religious fervour. Some of my views may seem irreligious at first sight. But a careful and scientific examination of the same will show that they are not actually so. I may however diverge from the popular and time-honoured, but in my opinion, misdirected beliefs regarding 'castes.' Caste system and religion are not necessarily connected with each other. So my ideas of 'caste' may differ from those of others, without in any way affecting the common religious sentiment. My views on the Ramayana have no concern with religion. But they are intimately connected with race distribution and 'caste' in the accepted sense of the word. To facilitate the enquiry, I propose to deal with the subject under three separate heads:— i. Race distribution and 'Caste' or rather the non-existence of 'caste' at the time of the Ramayana. ii. South Indian Castes prior to the time of the Ramayana. iii. South Indian Castes after the time of the Ramayana. SECTION I. South Indian Castes AT THE TIME OF THE RAMAYANA Of the two Ithihasas Ramayana and Bhārata , the latter is considered by some historians to have had some foundation on facts. But no historical incident has as yet been brought to light which could have supplied the ground-work for the construction of the story of the Ramayana .* 'Sita' and 'Rama' are used in the Vedas to mean 'furrow' and 'water' respectively. Linguists derive the words 'Aryar' and, '\sigmai' from the same root and say that 'Aryar' means 'എട്തെയാൻ' (those owning ploughs—agriculturists). On these data some historians look upon the Ramayana as an allegorical representation of the spread of Aryan civilization in India and the conquest of South India by the Aryans. As such, the Ramayana of Valmiki would be a poem written by an Aryan poet to proclaim the prowess of the Aryans. The merits of the Non-Aryans and the demerits of the Aryans as admitted by the Aryan poet need not be called in question. But where Valmiki mentions some prominent Dravidian princes † and enumerates the offences for which Rama fought against them, dethroned them and replaced them by men who would do his bidding, it would be worth while to enquire into the nature of the charges against the Dravidian * Even granting that the 'Ramayana' was founded on facts the general line of argument followed in this paper will not be affected. † The Dravidians in the poem are Vali, Sugriva, Hanuman and others of South India and Ravana, Vibheeshana, and others of Lanka. It does not stand to reason to suppose that these were monkeys and monsters as Valmiki would have us believe. princes deposed by Rama and the methods he adopted to conquer them. I. The two persons whom Valmiki accuses strongly are Ravana and Vali. (a) The charges brought against Ravana are :— i. that he incarcerated the Devas; ii. that he disturbed the peace of the Aryan 'munivars' (ascetics); and iii. that he abducted Sita. (b) The charges levelled against Vali are :— i. that he banished Sugriva; and ii. that he took Sugriva's wife to himself. II. The Aryan methods of conquest. Will be discussed later on. I. Valmiki's Culprits. i. Ravana. —The high culture and the manifold achievements of Ravana are extolled by Valmiki himself. Ravana was an enlightened monarch, learned in the Vedas , versed in the science and art of music, and withal formidable in the battle-field. He had subjugated many lands by the strength of his arm. His subjects enjoyed peace and prosperity under his rule. His relatives received at his hands a cordial and hospitable treatment. It is not clear what Valmiki meant by describing him as a ten-headed monster with twenty hands. Perhaps the poet intended thereby to impress upon the minds of his readers the high order of intelligence and the extreme physical strength of Ravana. Otherwise the description is altogether meaningless.* * Compare with the above, the remarks of Dr. G. Oppert in his "Original Inhabitants of India" (See p. p. 87 & 88). He writes. — "While Ravana is regarded with horror by the Brahmans, Rávanābhēt , a Vedic work on Phonetics , is ascribed to this Rakshasa. His memory is still cherished by the Jains. It is also curious that Ravana is esteemed and acknowledged by pious Pandits as a learned man, and is supposed to have been the author of a Telugu Grammar. Though the Rakshasas are ii. Vali. —Vali was a South Indian prince of wide-spread renown. His very conquest of Ravana is enough to proclaim his valour. A devout worshipper of Civa, he could admire even in his foes such virtues as obedience to parents, love towards brothers, loyalty to one's wife, faithfulness to promise, courage in the battle-field, etc. Such virtues he admired even in Rama, the enemy of his country and his race. So much in favour of Ravana and Vali. Let us now examine what Valmiki has to say against them. (a) The charges against Ravana i. The incarceration of the Devas :— The Devas were a section of the Aryan race. The Aryans gave the Dravidians the appellation of monkeys and monsters and styled themselves Suras ( \kappa \mu \hat{n} ) and Devas ( \kappa \text{g} \mathfrak{w} \hat{n} ), "gods." The Devas were thus a part of the Aryan race. If Ravana took captive a section of his foes, it is, to say the least, no detriment to his character. ii. Disturbing the peace of the 'munivars' :— The 'munivars' in question were Aryan ascetics who settled themselves in the Dravidian forests and acted as spies upon the Dravidians. The Dravidians tore off their mask of religion and banished them from their lands without meting out the extreme but justifiable punishment of death. Herein the generosity of the Dravidian nature is apparent. iii. The abduction of Sita:— When there is enmity or when war breaks out between two nations, it is customary for the one to sieze by force or described in the Ramayana and else-where as horrible both physically and morally, it appears that the condition of being a Rakshasa depended more upon the sins committed by an individual or by his progenitors than upon the accident of birth. If this be admitted, the physical monstrosities ascribed to the Rakshasas must be regarded as the exaggerated creations of a morbid and hostile imagination. Even the Ramayana extols the beauty and grandeur of Lanka, its architectural splendour, and the efficiency of its administration. This latter was so excellent, that no thief dared to pick up any valuable thing lost on its streets. The enemies of Rama could hardly, therefore, have been so rude and uncivilised as they are generally represented." [Ed.] stratagem the men, women, cattle, etc., belonging to the other. Now the Aryans were making their aggressive march upon the Dravidian kingdoms. And Ravana acted within his rights in imprisoning Sita. When Sita was in Lanka, she was treated with becoming princely dignity. She was placed in Asokavana , one of Ravana's best parks, with Ravana's own niece for her companion and several other maids for her attendants. Falling in love with her, Ravana pressed his suit for her hand, but he was never rude or ungentlemanly in his behaviour towards her. He would not, like a barbarian, force her into marriage with him. This is not all. Even when countless myriads of his army had lost their lives in the battle-field, even when his brother Kumbakarna and his son Indrajit had died in the fight, he would not in his blind rage destroy the life of his enemy's wife. It was not that the thought did not strike him. He thought of it and just to frighten Rama and Lakshmana he caused a lifelike effigy of Sita to be destroyed before their eyes. This is the treatment that the Aryan Sita received at the hands of the Dravidian Ravana. But how did the Dravidian Surpanaka fare at the hands of the Aryan Lakshmana? The spirit of chivalry shone in Lakshmana when he mutilated the nose and ears of Surpanaka. And to justify the abominable action, Valmiki gravely states that the woman tried to kidnap Sita in the presence of a man—Lakshmana. Even granting that she did try to do so, could not the victor of Indrajit* find less clumsy and more honourable methods of defeating her purpose? Did Rama at least feel sorry for the atrocity his brother had perpetrated? No. How could we expect a personage, who actually killed Thataka, feel com punction for the mere mutilation of the limbs of another woman. The abduction of Sita might have even been an act of vengeance on the part of Ravana for the injustice perpetrated * Indrajit, son of Ravana. 'Indrajit' literally means 'the victor of Indra' on his relative Thataka and his sister Surpanaka. If so, Ravana's action requires not even the shadow of a justification. The behaviour of Ravana towards Sita and the behaviour of Rama and Lakshmana towards Thataka and Surpanaka give one an insight into the treatment accorded to women by the Dravidians and Aryans respectively. The Dravidian and Aryan civilizations need not be compared further. And we need not wonder why the Dravidians considered the Aryans 'mlechas' or barbarians.* The description of Ravana's city, with its streets, palaces and parks, the educational attainments of men like Ravana and Hanuman, the reception accorded by Ravana to ambassadors like Hanuman and Angathan, the royal style of life allowed to Sita during the period of her imprisonment—all these go to indicate the state of Dravidian civilization as it then was. (b) The sins of Vali. Vali is accused of banishing his brother Sugriva and robbing him of his wife. Vali was by right of premogeniture the ruler of Kishkindha. He was for some time away-in foreign lands, Sugriva meanwhile acting as his representative in the kingdom. When Vali returned from his travels, Sugriva refused to hand over the reins of government and Vali had to fight for his crown. Eventually, Sugriva, Hanuman and other traitors were driven into exile. But their wives were allowed to remain in the land without molestation. These might have been the bare facts. There is reason to believe that Valmiki has distorted the facts favourably to Rama and Sugriva. If Sugriva did not seek his brother's life out of ambition for the crown, he would have, on Vali's death, enthroned Angathan, Vali's son, and the rightful heir to the throne. That Sugriva did not do so indicates clearly that he acted the regicide as well as the fratricide. A justification was needed for the conduct of Sugriva and Rama towards Vali. And it is probable that to supply the justification Valmiki invented the tale of Vali's coveting his brother's wife. * Vide the Tamil lexicon, 'Nigandu' ( Shācān ) of Mandala Purudar. II. The Aryan Methods of Conquest: i. The last words of Vali evince the high admiration he had for Rama. Vali was, besides, a valiant soldier. Under such circumstances one might reasonably ask why Rama preferred Sugriva's to Vali's friendship. As has already been hinted, Vali was strong enough to stand on his own legs. If Rama had befriended him, Vali would have reciprocated the sentiment. But certainly he would not have helped Rama, a foreigner and a new friend, against Ravana, an old friend and a Dravidian ruler like himself. With Sugriva it was otherwise. He was a benished prince and in need of help. It was likely that he would be grateful for any help offered at that juncture. Sugriva was moreover a man who had proved traitorous to his own brother. Such a man was not likely to shrink from taking the field against a Dravidian prince—Ravana—in favour of a foreign intruder—Rama. These were probably the motives that actuated Rama in befriending Sugriva and his followers and teaching them the Aryan military tatics. Rama did not however side with Sugriva openly and run the risk of losing Vali's good-will. In case Sugriva should lose in the fratricidal war, Rama had yet the chance of trying to persuade Vali to join him against Ravana. ii. We have seen how Rama made use of Sugriva for conquering Kishkindha. A similar stratagem was used in the case of Lanka also. Ravana's brother, Vibheeshana, was a willing tool in the hands of Rama. The Aryan writer Valmiki has endowed this Vibheeshana with many virtues in consideration of the latter's help to the Aryans against the best interests of his country and his race. The Dravidians of a later date have been foolish enough to follow Valmiki and dub Vibheeshana with the honorific title of Azhwar ( >> / <|335|> <|874|> <|413|><|874|><|714|><|874|><|714|><|914|><|893|><|954|><|954|><|674|><|587|><|90|> <|413|><|874|><|714|><|674|><|584|><|654|><|893|><|683|><|91|><|654|><|654|><|683|><|683|><|682|><|691|><|54|><|684|><|673|><|674|><|683|><|681|><|462|><|684|><|688|><|684|><|887|><|94|><|459|><|418|><|683|><|418|><|678|><|681|><|681|><|678|><|678|><|871|><|688|><|908|><|684|><|958|><|588|><|948|><|680|><|914|><|673|><|678|><|918|><|683|><|948|><|678|><|908|><|683|><|908|><|938|><|984|><|908|><|679|><|988|><|990|> Like Sugriva, Vibheeshana was a traitor and a fratricide in one. The only difference between these two persons lies in this that the latter possessed more cunning and less courage. The one tried to gain in open fight what his brother had obtained by right of primogeniture. The other tried to gain by low cunning and treachery the kingdom owned by his brother by right of conquest. Justly or unjustly, the one had been driven into exile by his brother: the other was kept in royal state by the bounty of his brother. Not satisfied with this, Vibheeshana aspired to become king and he sought the friendship of Rama. Valmiki contends that the unrighteous conduct of Ravana with reference to Sita was the root cause of the apostacy of Vibheeshana. It has already been noticed that the imprisonment of Sita casts no slur on Ravana's character. Even granting that the action was improper, that would be a reason for Vibheeshana's severing his connection with Ravana, and not for his acting the traitor to his country and his race. Like Vibheeshana, Kumbakarna and Indrajit pleaded the cause of Sita; but they did not like him leave Ravana in the lurch at the critical moment. They were quite prepared to fight to the death in the interests of their country and their sovereign. Kumbakarna's patriotism could not be shaken even by Vibheeshana's tempting and perhaps genuine offer of the throne of Lanka in the event of Ravana's demise in the battle-field. Vibheeshana's conduct is inexplicable on the ground that every patriot's duty is to rescue his country from the hand of oppression. Ravana might have caused trouble to the Devas and other Aryan sections, but mention is nowhere made in Valmiki of his having oppressed his subjects. What then induced Vibheeshana to debase himself at the feet of Rama and instruct him as to the vulnerable points of the Dravidian heroes? What, if not his ambition for the crown which manifested itself on Ravana's death. The then Social Condition of India. At the time of the Ramayana, the Aryans, it would seem, were just colonising South India. They had not yet entered into large cities. They built huts in the forests and lived in them. Caste differentiation does not seem to have existed either in South or in North India. We learn from the Ramayana that Rama with great respect and cordiality shook hands with Guha, a chief of the Nishadas, at the shores of the Ganges. It never entered his thoughts that his person might be polluted by the touch of a non-Aryan Nishada. We find again the royal guests in the house of the Vanara prince, in the Malaya hills of the South, freely moving, dining and sleeping in the midst of the courtiers of Sugriva, and fostering a brotherly feeling towards, and intimate union with, the latter prince. In their return journey to Ayodhya, we find Sita in the friendly company of Vanara ladies of high rank. We also find the royal members of Ayodhya accompanied by the brave Dravidian warriors to whose valour the victory was mainly due, entering the hermitage of the renowned Brahman Bharadvaja where a rich feast is provided for them. The Rakshasas, Vanaras, Brahmans and the royal household of Ayodhya sit together at table and partake freely of the good things placed before them. Nowhere do we find the slightest trace of that hated caste distinction—the curse of later-day India. The picture here given is that of the Social condition of the people of India three thousand years ago. If, then, the Aryan poet called other races ‘Monkeys,’ and ‘Monsters’ it indicates nothing else than the existence in him of a feeling of race hatred and contempt for neighbours. Assuming the historicity of the Ramayana, the geographical distribution of South India would be about the following. The country between the Vindhyas and the Nizam's dominions was known the eastern portion as Dandakaranya and the western as Janasthana. It was ruled by Sūrpanakhâ acting as the representative of Ravana. To the south of Janasthana and Dandakaranya, round Mysore, ruled the Dravidian kings Neelan, Vali, etc. The Tamilagam , “the home of the Tamils,” which lay to the south of Mysore, must have been a fertile country then. Special mention is made in Valmiki of Pandia's wealth.

title: The Ramayana: an Historical Study
author: P. V. Nanu Pillai
text: The Ramayana – An Historical Study.* BY MR. P. V. NANU PILLAI, B.A. Of all the great literary productions of ancient India none is more widely popular or is more generally appreciated by Hindus of all classes and of different degrees of intelligence than the Ramayana of Valmiki. There are greater and even sublimer works, such as the Vedas and the Upanishads. But none of them except the Mahabharatha can be said to be so well-known to and appreciated by the people at large. Even the Mahabharatha is not so much an epic poem, as it is an encyclopædia of ancient Hindu legends and folklore, collected and collated by successive authors known by the general designation of Vyasa. Further it is an unwieldy work, perhaps the longest poetical work in the World. The Ramayana, on the other hand, is the work of a single author, Valmiki, justly known as the Adikavi or the first poet. He is not merely first in the order of time, but first also in the order of merit. Of all the epic poems in the world, the Ramayana stands unparalleled. Its peculiar fascination lies in the compactness of the story, in the chasteness and the simplicity of its language, in the loftiness of its ethics and above all in the religious instruction which it imparts to its votaries. The word Rama is a household name in every Hindu family. It has such significance to the Hindu mind that it is almost synonymous with the name of God—so much so that the very uttering of the word, a number of times, constitutes a round of prayer in the case of an ordinary Hindu. The word Rama is derived from the word ram which means to please , and it is used in the sense of Atmaram , i.e., that which pleases the soul. * The Editor desires it to be understood that, in printing this paper in the Tamilian Antiquary, he does not accept any responsibility for the views expressed by the writer. The paper is reprinted by kind permission from the "Malabar Quarterly Review" only as showing the different aspects of this much-discussed question. It is therefore no wonder, that the epic poem which celebrates the deeds of Rama has so much charm to the Hindu mind. It is to the Hindus what the Bible is to the Christians, the Koran to the Mohammadans, the Avesta to the Parsis and the Bodhisathwa to the Buddhists. The story of the Ramayana is a simple one and a brief summary of it, in as few words as possible, will be a fitting introduction to the subject of this paper, as in the course of our discussion, frequent allusion has to be made to it. Dasaratha, king of Ayoshya, is afflicted with the sad thought that he has no son and the reflection Aputrasyagatir-nasti , “the sonless have no salvation” makes him quite miserable. With a view to beget a son to whom to bequeathe the kingdom which has had an uninterrupted line of succession, he performs a great yagam to propitiate the gods. Pleased with its austerity, they bless him with four sons. The eldest of these, born of Kausalya one of the three consorts of the king, was called Rama. The next one Bharatha, was born of Kaikeyi. Sumithra gave birth to the twins Lakshmana and Sathrughna. When Rama came of age, King Dasaratha made preparations to install him on his throne and seek rest in forest which his growing years and the custom of his country rendered necessary. Jealous of the preference shown by the Raja to the son of Kausalya, Kaikeyi demands of the King the fulfilment of a promise made by him in former days that her wishes would be gratified whatever they might be and whenever they were pressed forward. The King to whom truth is the highest law of being and justice is an application of it to human affairs, complies at once with Kaikeyi's request, to banish Rama to the forest and to install his son Bharatha instead. Thus Rama goes into the woods followed by his beloved wife Sita and his faithful brother Lakshmana. They wander in the forest from hermitage to hermitage for about ten years when they settled down near Nasik. At this time Ravana, King of Rakshasas, visits the hermitage of Rama during his absence and stealthily takes Sita into his aerial car and carries her away to Lanka. The brothers then set out from there in quest of Sita, form an alliance with Sugriva, the King of the Monkeys, get across to the island of Ceylon, engage Ravana in battle, vanquish him outright, recover Sita and return to Ayodhya where Sri-Rama was crowned as King. The Ramayana like many other Indian epics is a story founded on solid facts of history. It is a history of the Aryan colonisation of South India. If by history is meant a correct record of the doings of the people at any period of their life, their habits, manners and customs, their mode of living, their way of fighting, the causes of their wars, the weapons they used in battles, the religions they professed, the ethics they followed and the gods they worshipped, we have in the Ramayana, copious materials which will afford a faithful history of the Indian people at a period long anterior to the Christian era. The poem begins with the description of Ayodhya and an eulogium on Dasaratha and his ministers. The city of Ayodhya is described as being situate on the banks of the river Sarayu, studded with forts and fortresses, with towers and palaces. The city is peopled by the different orders of society, the Brahmans, the Kshathrias, the Vaisyas and the Sudras. The Brahmans were treated with the highest respect. The Kshathriyas occupied a position next in rank to the Brahmans. The Vaisyas formed a common folk. The Sudras were serfs in the employ of the other three classes. They were the descendants of the conquered aborginal races not much advanced in civilisation and were naturally treated therefore as servants. Dasaratha had eight ministers of the cabinet, all of them being Brahmans. Vasishta and Vamadeva were the foremost of them. Of the eight members, Purohita was the chief family priest and religious adviser to the king answering to the Archbishop of Canterbury. Next comes the Prathinidhi , the Ambassador; next in order is the Pradana or the Prime minister. The next is Suchina or the War minister. Then comes Manthri or the Chief Counsellor. Praswivaku or the Chief Judge of the Privy Council; Pandita the expert in Sruthis and Smrithis and Sumantharaka or the Private Secretary to the King, make up the cabinet of those days in strict conformity with the ordinance of Manu. The poet next describes the grief of Dasaratha on account of his being heirless. The next chapters deal with the birth of the children and their early training. They studied the Vedas and the Sastras before the age of sixteen. Intellectually and morally therefore they had no superiors. In physical pursuits also they were trained from their infancy. They were the sons of a king and as such they were trained in the use of swords and arrows and in all other manly exercises. In fact they did not neglect one branch of education to the detriment of the other. They bestowed the greatest attention upon the training of the body which we in these days of degeneration do not care for. They realised the principle that without a healthy body, healthy morality and healthy intellect were impossible. From these facts you will see how fallen the modern Hindus are in their notion of education. The poet next goes on to describe the Swayamvaram of Sita, and the intrigues at the Court of Ayodhya by reason of which Rama is banished into the Dekhan which is described as a huge forest inhabited by races unfriendly to the Aryas. Coming to the South of India, the poet brings us face to face with no less than half a dozen different varieties of humanity. First, we are introduced to Guha, who is described as the head of a nomadic race of people who lived upon the roots and fruits of the forests and upon the flesh of wild animals which they hunted. They had no houses but dwelt under the shades of trees or in temporary huts thatched with leaves. They were not unfriendly to the Aryans, but acknowledged their superiority. The depth of contempt in which these people were held by the Aryans may be seen from the fact that Bharata becomes astonished to hear that Sri-Rama shook hands with Guha. That Sri-Rama should pollute his person by the touch of an unclean Kiratha was really a matter of wonder and surprise to his brother Bharata. Going still more south into the Dekhan the poet brings to our view, the cannibal Viradha whom Rama kills. The poet gives us only one or two instances of cannibals whom Sri-Rama is said to have slain. The fact is that when the Aryan colonization of South India began, they found some places inhabited by cannibals whom they at once destroyed. Next we are introduced to the great Rakshasas and the Monkey races . As I have already said, the story of the Ramayana is a history of the Aryan colonization of South India. Sri-Rama, though he is a single individual should not be treated as such. He is simply the representative of the Aryan people who have colonised the countries of South India as far as Nasik. To the south of Nasik lay the great Rakshasa kingdom and a little to the east was the Kingdom of the Monkeys. These Monkeys and Rakshasas should not be looked upon as quadrumana or demons. They represented the two prominent races of South India at the time of the Ramayana. The Rakshasas as their name indicates were a fierce race of people who scorned the supremacy of the Aryans and had withstood all their attempts to aryanize them through long ages. They occupied the countries to the south of Nasik on the west coast of India. This country extended up to Cape Comorin and thence to Ceylon. They were a considerably civilised people. They were armed with swords and spears. The science of archery was also known to them. But they excelled in the use of swords. They were perhaps acquainted with the sea and knew the art of navigation. Their Chief is said to have had an aerial car. They had a feudal system among themselves consisting of petty lords or generals who followed their king whenever called upon to do so. They were not illiterate. Their Chief, Ravana, is said to have been conversant with the Vedas and the Sastras. He had a fortress in his city of Lanka which is described as impregnable. He had two brothers whom he treated as his colleagues. He had his uncles also of whom we hear only in the first part of the story. They seem to have governed the country of Hindustan near Nasik; for they were the first to take the field against Rama to chastise him for the mutilation of Sūrpanakhâ. Ravana had two or three sons of whom Indrajit is the foremost. He is the eldest but in no place is he treated as the heir-apparent. He is treated rather as a favoured general. Ravana had a sister to whom is ascribed the cause of the war. She had a husband first who died; and she seems to have had children by him. But she was young and wanted to re-marry. The Rakshasa women were free to choose their husbands. As she was wandering in the outskirts of the empire she met with two handsome youths from the north; and naturally she felt an inclination towards them. But they mutilated her. Coming next to the Monkey race as they were called, we find them to be a partially civilized people having their king, their government, their ministers and officers. They had a fort in which were the houses of their chiefs and their dependants. Their king Bâli is described as a powerful chief, who was feared by all. He is also a religious man and used to say his morning and evening prayers regularly. This king had an army which was large, but they had no weapons except clubs and sticks. They were a strong and well-built people. They had a settled system of inheritance. But they were mostly black and were, probably on that account, called Monkeys by the Aryans. They seem to have been the descendants of an Assyrian race of people who entered India at a very remote time. They were the worshippers of Surya or the Sun. Their king Bâli worshipped this deity in the morning and evening. Their other chief Sugriva is called the son of Surya and Hanuman their minister is said to have been a pupil of the same deity. These facts go to prove that they were an Assyrian colony that settled in India from time immemorial. They were a peace-loving race and were mostly vegetarians living upon fruits and roots. They had heard of the powers of the Aryanized Kshatrias and had taken to learning their language. Hanuman is described as speaking the Sanskrit language with a fluency and accent that astonished the brothers Rama and Lakshmana. They were therefore easily brought under the Aryan influence and turned out to be a great source of strength to the Aryans in the war that followed. Now that I have given a description of the Rakshasas and the Monkeys and have made the reader understand that they were men like ourselves, let me resume the thread of my narrative. The Aryans, I have told had colonized all countries to the north of Nasik; and to the south of Nasik lay the kingdom of the Rakshasas. These Aryans were an agricultural people, and wherever they went they reclaimed forests and tilled the soil. They lived upon the milk of their cattle and the produce of their soil; occasionally they used to hunt and eat of the venison. Their chief was called Rama or Sri-Rama which name is perhaps identical with the Hali-Rama of the Mahabharata. Hali-Rama means the Rama with the plough and as such is a typical Aryan farmer. His wife was called Sita which again means a furrow and is again symbolical of Aryan agriculture. In the borders of their colony they frequently came in contact with the Rakshasas and had on one occasion maltreated their women having cut off their noses and ears. Ravana, the king of Rakshasas, was duly informed of this outrage and he soon came to chastize the enemy. He planned a novel mode of campaign. He knew the Aryans to be good archers and perhaps knew his own weakness also. He therefore called in the aid of Maricha who is described as assuming the form of a golden deer and enticing away the brothers, Rama and Lakshmana. This golden deer is again symbolical of wild cattle. Maricha collected a herd of wild cattle and let them loose on the crops of the Aryans. Seeing that their crop was in danger of being destroyed all the male members went to the rescue of the same. In the meanwhile, Ravana and his followers entered their houses and carried away their implements of agriculture and all their women. When the male members returned home they found their homes plundered and deserted. They at once set out in search of their women and property. They first met with Jadayu who is described as a bird, but who in reality was the typical pariah slave of the period. He was not given entrance into the houses of the Aryans, but was allowed to live at a respectable distance from the residence of his lords. He lived upon the carcasses of men and animals. But with all that he was a faithful servant; and as such he did his best to save the women and property of his master. But he was no match to Ravana who at once cut him down with his sword. He just lived long enough to tell the story of the kidnapping of Sita. Then the poet describes the search of Sita by Rama and Lakshmana. After many adventures, they meet with Hanuman, the minister of Sugriva. Sugriva was driven away from his kingdom by his brother Bâli and was living as an exile in the forest. So there was much of mutual sympathy between Rama and Sugriva. They enter into alliance as a sequel to which Bâli is killed in battle by Rama and the kingdom of Kishkindha is given over to Sugriva. Rama and Sugriva then find out the whereabouts of Sita and attempt to cross the Ocean. At this time Vibhishana, the traitor-brother of Ravana privately sees Rama and enters into a secret alliance with him. With the powerful assistance of Sugriva and with the no less powerful support of Vibhishana, Rama crosses over to Ceylon, engages Ravana in battle, kills him and all his men and installs Vibhishana as King of the Rakshasas. Vibhishana in gratitude for his leige-lord takes Sita back and places her at his feet. After this Rama returns home and reigns as sovereign. Here ends practically the story of the Ramayana. From the account just now given you will find that by this war, the whole of South India including Ceylon was subdued by the Aryans and that these countries were in due course completely Aryanized. I have now told you that the History of the Ramayana was the history of a war between the aryanized Kshatriyas of the North and the non-aryanized Rakshasas of the South. In this war the Rakshasa power was completely subdued, their kingdom being made tributary to the Empire of Ayodhya. The downfall of the Rakshasas was due partly to intrigues among themselves and partly to the powerful support the Aryans derived from the Assyrian inhabitants of India but mostly to the mental and moral superiority of the Aryans. Now the question may naturally arise as to who these Rakshasas were. Were they Kshatrias? Or, as such were they a branch of the Aryan people? Did they belong to the Monkey race? Were they a separate race of people differing from all these? Are they in these days represented by any peoples of India? For this purpose we have to draw a comparison between the races already treated of. First let us proceed with the question whether the Rakshasas were Monkeys and try to answer it. 1. The Monkeys are described as vegetarians, which the Rakshasas were not. 2. The Monkeys though they were a strong and well-built people were not as fierce and war-like as the Rakshasas. 3. The Monkeys were a peace-loving people. But the Rakshasas if they loved anything at all, loved war. 4. Hanuman and Sugriva are described as men almost resembling Monkeys. But Ravana is described as Daçahasya that is a double Panchahasya , which means broad-faced. 5. Bali and Sugriva worshipped the sun. But Ravana and his people worshipped Civa. 6. The Monkeys were not much learned as the Rakshasas. Ravana is said to be conversant with the Vedas and the Sastras. 7. The Monkeys had no weapons except clubs and stones. But the Rakshasas were skilled in the use of swords and spears. They knew also the art of archery. 8. The Monkeys lived in an inland country and were afraid of the ocean when they first saw it. The Rakshasas lived, some of them at least, beyond the ocean and knew the art of navigation. 9. The Rakshasas in spite of their being fierce were a more civilized people than the Monkeys. 10. The Monkeys had a system of inheritance which was from father to son. But the Rakshasas had no settled system. Ravana gets his kingdom not from his father who was a Brahman sage; but he inherits his kingdom through his mother's ancestors. Again Ravana's kingdom goes to his brother and not to his son. 11. Lastly nowhere is it said in the Ramayana that these two peoples were inter-related. In fact the Rakshasas despised the Monkeys as did the Kshatriyas also. Now let us see whether these Rakshasas were Kshatriyas and as such Aryans. 1. They were like the Kshatriyas a warlike people. 2. Their women like the Kshatriyas were free to choose their husbands. 3. They like the Kshatriyas worshippped Civa. Almost all the Civa temples in Northern India are ascribed to the Prathishta of Janaka and other Kshatriya kings. The Civa temples in South India are ascribed to the Prathishta of Kara and other Rakshasas. 4. It was the custom among the ancient Kshatriyas when any family was going to become extinct, to beget children in Kshatriya women by Brahmans. This practice was followed in the case of Ravana. 5. Among the ancient Kshatriyas Polyandry and Polygamy prevailed as may be seen from the stories in the Mahabharata. The Rakshasas were also subject to this custom. 6. The Rakshasas used to do penance as did the Kshatriya kings. But when a Sudra did it, he was punished with death by Sri-Rama. 7. Again the Kshatriyas of the Mahabharata are described as having Asura blood in them. Whence did they get this Asura blood if they did not belong primarily to the Asura stock? In all these respects the Kshatriyas and the Rakshasas agree. Let us now see wherein they differ. 1. The Kshatriyas professed caste and acknowledged the social superiority of the Brahmans which the Rakshasas did not. 2. The Kshatriyas had a fixed system of inheritance which, we have shewn, the Rakshsas had not. 3. The Kshatriyas performed yagas or Brahman rites which the Rakshasas made it a rule to obstruct. 4. The Rakshasas though they were once polyandrous and polygamous had become entirely mono-androus and monogamous at the time of the Ramayana. These are the points of difference. But the points of agreement are more numerous and important than the points of difference which may be explained away by saying that Kshatrias had completely aryanized themselves under the moral influence of the Brahmans. Now a theory may be formulated which I hope will explain the complete aryanisation of the Kshatrias. The Aryan Brahmans entered India not as conquerors but as spiritual teachers. For they, even to this day, trace their descent from some spiritual Guru or Rishi. These Gurus were headed by a religious chief called Manu; and there were a number of successive Manus whose duty it was to make laws and regulations for the conduct and guidance of their followers from time to time. These laws and regulations are what are known as the Manava Dharma Sastras. The mission of the Aryans was thus at first a peaceful one. But in course of time they were forced to take up arms, just as the English merchants later on were forced to do so for their defence. These Aryans were mentally and morally the superiors of the peoples that inhabited India at that time. These latter belonged either to an earlier wave of the Aryan exodus to the south or to the kindred family of the Semitics or were probably a mixed race composed of both. But all accounts go to shew that they were a people closely allied to the Aryans. They were the worshippers of Civa and the idols and were probably divided into three orders of society but not into castes, the then orders being the king and their followers, the landlords and merchants and the serfs or servants. It was at this juncture that the Aryas entered India just as it was when the Hindus were divided into four castes that the Mahomedans invaded the country. The Puranas and Itihasas describe the struggle that was going on for long ages between these Aryas and the non-Aryanized peoples of India. Many of these latter were in due course completely aryanised and were called Manavas or the followers of Manu. The term Manava was at first a term of contempt applied by the natives of India to denote a follower of Manu just as the term Christian was a term of contempt applied originally by the Ancient Jews to denote a follower of Christ. The Manavas were divided into four castes as the Brahmans, Kshatrias, Vysyas and Sudras of whom the Brahmans or Bhusuras were the descendants of those Rishis, who entered India for proselytizing, while the remaining castes were taken from society as it was then existing in India. But apart from these four castes, there remained a fifth class of people made up entirely of the natives of India who preferred to worship their own gods rather than submit to the gods of the Aryans. These people fled to the South of India and were called by the Aryas as Asuras and Rakshasas which terms originally meant only the ungodly or the infidel as opposed to the Aryas who were called the Suras, the godly or faithful people by pre-eminence. With the advance of the Aryans and the aryanized natives southwards the Asuras also receded until at last all the plains of India and even Ceylon came into the Aryan possession. These Asuras and Rakshasas are then described as taking shelter in a place called Pâthâlam. It is from the confines of this Pathala that Malayavan the father of Kykesi is described as going out in search of a kinsman to marry his daughter. But finding none, he marries her to the Rishi Visravas by whom she gets three sons Ravana, Kumbhakarna and Vibhishna. When these princes grew up they regained their lost possession of Lanka and re-asserted their former predominance. It was to destroy this predominance that the Ramayana war was undertaken and the precautions taken by the Aryans to completely overthrow the rising Rakshasa power correspond exactly with the precautions taken by the English in order to subdue the rising Mahomedan power of Tippu. Now one word about Pâthâla and I have done with this historical aspect. Where was this Pathala? Was it an under-ground world or was it any country in India itself? I say it is no under-ground world. It was some place in South India itself where the non-Aryanized population of India took final shelter. Let us then see what part of South India corresponds, exactly with the description of the Pathala mentioned in the Puranas. I think that the country bounded on the east by the Western Ghats, on the north by the mountains near Nasik and on the west and south by the sea was probably the Pathala of the Puranas. The synonyms for Pathala are Adhobhuvana 'an under-ground world;' Balisatma , 'the country of Mahabali,' the Asura chief; Nagaloka 'the country of the serpents;' and Kuhara 'a cave.' This country on the Malabar Coast which I have mentioned is the only place even now for a pursued army to take final shelter in South India. It was not known to the Aryans until a very late period. The Ramayana professes to be entirely ignorant of the countries South of Nasik. This country is called even to this day as Papa-Bhumi, 'the country of the Papis or Barbarians', by the Hindus. It is an under-ground world when looked down from the Western Ghats. It is again at the foot of the world when viewed from the hills. It is this country in which even to this day the memory of an Asura chief is cherished with joy and enthusiasm. Onam and other festive days are all in commemoration of the ideal Asura king Mahabali. In no other part of India we will find the memory of an Asura chief so much cherished. Again the Malabar Coast is the abode of serpents by pre-eminence. It is noted for the number and variety of its serpents. In no part of the world will you find serpents being worshipped as in Malabar. No other country of the world can boast of special serpent priests called Pullavars even to this day. These Pullavars are perhaps the descendants of a serpent worshipping people who were subdued by the Asuras. The present Nairs are probably the descendants of those Asura warriors who defied the power of the Aryans in the plains and who, when they found that resistance was hopeless to defend the plains, sent first their women and children into the country beyond the Ghats and stationed powerful military guards in all the passes that opened the country to the outer-world. The present Sasta temples stationed at the entrance to these passes were temples of Civa, originally established by the Asura armies for their worship. Even the “Keralolpathi” acknowledges that these Sasta temples were instituted for the purpose of preventing the influx of the Aryan Brahmans from the plains. All these facts more than bear out the truth of my statement that the country described as Pathala in the Puranas is the country of the Malabar Coast. The long absence of the male members from home for defending their country and upholding their tradition led in due course to a system of matriarchal government of properties among these warlike Asuras which had developed into the Marumakkathayam law after the entire annihilation of the Asura forces in the battle of Lanka. Now I have explained to you the common origin of the Rakshasas and the Kashatrias. It is my duty to prove that the commonly accepted theory that the Kshatrias were Aryans, who entered India along with the Brahmans, is a mistake. The surest test of kinship is inter-marriage. The very fact that there were from the beginning no inter-marriages between the Brahmans and the Kshatrias proves beyond the shadow of a doubt that they belonged either to two distinct races or at least to two different branches of the same race. If inter-marriage was current before the time of Manu, none of the Manus or no amount of legislation could have been able to check it. In fact legislation prohibiting inter-marriage would have been simply impossible. Again, the Vedic Brahmans never worshipped Civa. The name of Civa is not even mentioned in the oldest parts of the Vedas. The contempt in which this deity was held by the Brahmans may be seen from the fact that they even to this day do not partake of the food placed at the altar of Civa. The reason alleged for this attitude of the Brahmans is that Civa was a Brahman-killer. What does this mean? If it means anything at all, it is that Civa was a God of another religion entirely opposed to and subversive of Brahmanism. To show the moral purpose of the Ramayana I need only point out to you the various aspects in which the several characters in it are delineated. The person of Sri-Rama is always held out as the highest type of man. Whether as a son or pupil, or as a brother or friend, or as husband or father, or as an ally or enemy, or as a king or sage in whatever aspects he is viewed the figure of Sri-Rama stands out pre-eminently as among the highest ideals of humanity. Coming to the character of Sita, she is held out as the highest ideal of womanhood. In spite of being placed in adverse circumstances, in spite of being exposed to imminent dangers, and at the sight of death, she preserves her equanimity of temper and is never swayed by any other consideration than firm devotion to her lord. As to the character of Bharata, Lakshmana and Satrughna each of them excels the other in their devotion to their brother. I shall close this aspect of the Ramayana with a quotation. When Bharata finds out in the forests Sri-Rama and compels him to return home these are the words that formed his answer:—“There is nothing greater than truth and truth should be esteemed the most esteemed of all things. The Vedas have their sole foundation on truth. Having promised obedience to my father’s commands I will never through covetousness or forgetfulness or blind ignorance break down the barrier of truth.”

title: Studies in the Ramayana: the Geography and Ethnology of the Poem
author: C. Tirumalayya Naidu
text: STUDIES IN THE RAMAYANA. BY Mr. C. TIRUMALAYYA NAIDU, M. R. A. S. THE GEOGRAPHY AND ETHNOLOGY OF THE POEM. A knowledge of geography and an ethnological survey of the country comprised in the Ramayana will be found to be necessary for an elucidation of many an intricate situation occurring in the poem. In the words of Mr. Cust, 'the glimpses of geographical knowledge afore-said of the poet are highly interesting to trace out; and the insight gained into the habits and manners of the people at the time the poem was written is invaluable.' The geography of the poem may not always be credible: but it is interesting as showing the extent and accuracy of the knowledge possessed by the poet. It is curious to find that, though the whole continent of what is now known as India was roughly known to the poet, he nowhere refers to it as a single whole, nor does he give any separate name for it. The name India is said to be derived from the Greek and the Roman adaptation of the word Hindu, which was used by the Persians for their Aryan brethren, because the latter settled in the districts surrounding the streams of the Sindhi (pronounced by them Hindu and now called Indus). The words Bharatavarsha and Aryavarta do not occur in the poem. The latter was the name given by Manu to the region between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains. Bharata was the most famous ruler of the Lunar dynasty and reigned at Hastinapura, the modern Delhi, over a more or less large part of India, which was henceforth known after his name. The poem opens with a description of the Kosala country on the bank of the Sarayu, the modern Gogra, which is supposed to have had its origin in the lake Manasaras, in the Himalayas. Although Ayodhya, its capital, whose extent was twelve yojanas in length and three in breadth (a yojana varying from four to eight miles) was 'the base of operations in the story, still the poet takes us through a vast extent of country, conducting us now beyond the Sutlej into the Panjab, now across the Vindhya mountains into the Dekhan, and now across the Narmada and Godavari to the most southern parts of India, even to the island of Ceylon.' Ikshwaku was its first king, and ruled over a large territory of land, which was known as 'Ikshwaku's dominions,' under which name Rama conveniently includes the country known as Kishkindha and ruled by Vali ( Vide Kishkindha Kânda, Sarga 18 and Sloka 6 ). Though Daçaratha boasted to Kaikeyi that his dominions extended as far as 'the wheel of the sun' could go, still he explicitly referred to countries like Sindhu, Savari, Sourashtra, Dakshinapatha, Vanga, Anga, Maghadha, Matsya, Kasi, and Kosala , over which he claimed a sort of suzerainty, from which he offered to get whatever she might be inclined to command! (Ayodhya Kânda, Sarga X, Sloka 37). But we know that Anga was ruled by Romapada, whom he mentions as his friend. But the invitations which Daçaratha issued on the occasion of his great horse sacrifice were confined to the rulers of Mithila, Kasi, Kêkaya, Anga, Sindhu, Savari and Sourashtra, and to many other nameless kings (Bala Kânda, Sarga XIII, Slokas 21 to 25 ). The poet's knowledge of this part of the country namely, the region to the north of the Vindhya, is more or less complete and the description of the whole country as detailed by Viswamithra to Rama on their way to Mithila is wonderfully minute. But beyond this, there was the great Dandaka forest infested with deadly reptiles and ferocious beasts of prey, and inhabited by cannibalistic Rakshasas. On the other side of the Sarayu, lived the tribe of the Nishadas, a race of pygmies, whose ruler was Guha and whose capital was Sringibera . An unbiassed study of the poem cannot but convince the reader that the great and perpetual struggle between the Rishis and the Rakshasas was the result of the aggressive colonization by the former, of the territories which were already under the unquestioned occupation of the latter. The great alluvial plains of the south, and the splendid possibilities of colonization in the continuous and beautiful forest with its myriads of flowering plants and fruit trees, and abounding in all sorts of wild game, and with its flowing rivers full of lotuses and lilies and of many varieties of edible fish, very early attracted the Rishis who founded amidst unceasing opposition, many hermitages which were innocently so called but which were really bases of operation against the accredited inhabitants of the plains. What was known as the Siddhasrama , originally belonged to the Emperor Bali, probably a very early ruler of the place who was, by inexcusable cunning and under the pretence of mendicancy, subjugated by Vishnu in the guise of a dwarf. Thus probably arose the feuds between the subjects of Bali and these aggressive colonists. Viswamitra whose permanent abode was on the bank of the Kowsi in the Himalayas makes it convenient to come down to the place for performing a sacrifice, although nothing prevented him from doing the same in his own asrama and in a more peaceful manner befitting his religious order. The Rakshasas naturally represented this unjustifiable intrusion, which necessitated his applying to Daçaratha for help. Many such hermitages were already founded and were known by the names of those Rishis who, more boldly than others, took to adventures of this kind. These were known as Bharadwaju Asrama, Sarabhanga Asrama, Atri Asrama, Sutikishna Asrama, Matanga Asrama, Agastya Asrama, &c. Beyond these Asramas, there was Janastana , the modern Naśik, which was probably the northern confines of Ravana's realm, where was quartered a large contingent of his army, headed by his own brothers Khara and Dusana , with a view apparently to keep watch over the determined incursions of the Rishis, and of their docile warrior rulers who were only too ready to carry out whatever they were bidden to do by the Rishis. The Ramayana is nothing but the history of the attempted colonization of a strange country by the Rishis and of the feuds which these bold incursions naturally gave rise to. Far down in the south, on the banks of the Pamoâ lake, there was the principality of Kishkindha, of which Vâli was the ruler. An attempt was made by the poet to put in the mouth of Sugriva a description of the early geography of the world, which is, however, most unreliable, owing to its hopeless exaggerations. But it is interesting to find mention thereof Cheena (China) in the north, which probably supplied, from the earliest times, the best silks, which formed the chief raiment of the aristocratic classes. But more trust-worthy is the description of the countries near the Godavery, and the Andhra, Pundra, Chola, Pandya and Kerala kingdoms in the south, where grew the stately cocoa-nut and sandal-wood trees in luxurious abundance. The banks of the Kaveri and Tambraparni are also referred to as the places where the search party headed by Angada and Hanuman sojourned for a time before they found a clue to the island of Lanka. Far more instructive is the study of the characteristics of the races of men that came in contact with each other in the course of the story. Broadly speaking, there were the Kshatriya race of the Solar descent, with their family preceptors the Rishis (who were not all Brahmins), the Nishadas, the Vanaras of the Central India, and the so-called Rakshasas who perpetually collided with their militant brethren of the North. The hero of the poem belonged to the Solar race whose origin is traced from Brahma through the Sun-god. But, for all practical purposes, Ikshwaku was the great ancestor who founded the dynasty known after his name. This race was characterised by all those qualities of the head and heart which go to make a great nation. A great line of worthy rulers, their rule was characterised by wise statesmanship and righteous conduct, which endeared them to their subjects. 'But the Rishis who were their family priests, and secular advisers as well, early succeeded in encouraging the growth of a sort of superstitious awe for, and in fostering an ever-increasing and servile dependence on, themselves for good and evil alike. The superstitious rulers feared their wrath, though heroic by nature and wise by culture. The Rishis, on their part, showed an inordinate zeal and anxious concern for their welfare and fame. In fact, the solar race owed its glorious successes as well as its ignominious failures to the machinations of these learned men. So far as internal economy was concerned, the Rishis, it must be said to their credit, were eminent for their impartiality, fair-mindedness and justice which was evenly administered between man and man. But, in the management of 'foreign affairs,' they hopelessly lacked that equitableness and fairness which alone secured peace. It was the Rishis that developed the plot which ultimately brought Rama into violent contact with the Rakshasas. When the latter requested their help in finding for him a suitable place in the forest where he could conveniently bide his time during the period of his self-exile, they strategically took him from place to place, till they pointed out Janastana as the best residential quarter for him. He did not know that it was a place thickly populated by the fierce-looking Rakshasas, till he met Sūrpanakha in one of her aimless wanderings. He was looked upon by her with suspicion which soon changed into fierce lust provoked by his handsome person. This part of the story is too well-known to need any recapitulation here. After the obstruction of the whole army of the Rakshasas, the Rishis approached him highly elated at his success and informed him with unconcealed satisfaction that he was most cunningly lured on to this place by them for the purpose of exterminating the cruel and sinful Rakshasas: ( Vide Aranya Kanda, Sarga XXX and Sloka 31) Rama only too fully realized this, after Sita was taken from him. (Aranya Kanda, Sarga 57, Sloka 9.) They, while jealous of their own possessions, were victim to that 'earth hunger' which really proved a bar to an otherwise just rule. The Nishadas were an insignificant people who played a very minor part in the development of the story. The Monkey-tribes, known as the Vânaras, occupied the central plateau of India and were conspicuous for their valour. Their colonies seem to have extended far and wide. Modern research has shown that they belonged to the Kolarian race, which probably represents the earliest settlers in India, whose country was later on encroached upon by the Dravidian races, who were sometimes friendly and sometimes inimical to them. Their stage of civilization could be inferred by the knowledge of the arts displayed by them as described by the poet. It was perhaps their dark and ugly features, smallness of stature, flattened nose, hairy growth and predatory habits, and their occupation of jungly and marshy tracts, shunning the haunts of men that had brought upon them the contempt of their fellow-beings. The Rakshasas are represented as the most hated of the Rishis whom they were not tired of molesting. But the poet showed no prejudice in delineating their characteristics. He displays true historical insight when he depicted them as belonging to a civilization which was in no way inferior to that of the Solar race itself. Occasional relapses into hyperbolical digressions on the part of the poet, such as the representation of the three-headed Trisiras , the ten-headed Ravana, the ever-sleepy Kumbakarna, the hideous Surpanakha, were probably intended to excite the flagging interest of the varied readers of this ponderous work with its inevitable repetitions. In the same way, in describing races unknown to the Greeks, such as the Cyclopes, Laestrogones, Centouræ, &c., Homer and other Greek writers are given to exaggeration and relate the most absurd tales. But the Rakshasas seem to have been an enlightened race, whose pugnacity and vindictiveness were due to the provocative depredations of the later Aryan settlers, but who were peaceful citizens in their own country, when left to themselves unmolested and unharassed. (Aranya Kanda, Sarga XXXVIII, Sloka 24). When Sita heard that Rama had peldged himself at any cost to protect the Rishis from the molestations of the Rakshasas, she very rightly tried her best to dissuade him from undertaking hostilities on their behalf, for which he could plead no sort of justification. She tells him that “an attempt to fight others unprovoked, is one of the three afflictions which man brings on himself by his own wantonness. I do not like the very idea of your entering the forest inhabited by the Rakshasas. I do not like that lives should be sacrificed without any cause for provocation. It is incumbent on you to practise the duty prescribed for those who have vowed to spend their lives in peaceful contemplation. You will please my father-in-law and mother-in-law by following such a duty.” (Aranya Kanda, Sarga IX, Slokas 3½ to 32½.) A very sound advice which Rama, however, preferred not to follow because of the promise he had already made to them, without any forethought of the consequences of such an action. In Lanka some of the Rakshasas were very handsome, wise, learned in arts and skilled in Vedic lore. But for his blind and unquenchable lust, Ravana was himself great not only by his vast learning and erudition but also by his tremendous valour and intrepidity which he displayed fearless of its after-results, and which provoked the admiration of his honest foes. There can be no doubt that these Rakshasas were the earliest Aryan settlers in India * which could be proved from the various Aryan customs and manners prevalent among them as described by Valmiki. It is very probable that as Monier Williams thinks, soon after their final occupation of the Gangetic districts, a body of invaders headed by a bold leader such as Ravana, might have forced their way far down into the south of India and into Ceylon. It was as mentioned above, the aggressive spirit of the later Aryan incursionists that was the cause of the conflict between the two branches of the same Aryan stock. * See note by the Editor in the following page. The Rakshasas—A Note. Mr. C. Tirumalayya Naidu's statement that the Rakshasas were the earliest Aryan settlers in India and were a branch of one and the same Aryan stock, seems to be deduced from the fact of their customs and manners resembling those of the Aryans. But there are many points in the Ramayana itself which clearly assign to the Rakshasas a different nationality. They certainly differed from the Aryan invaders as to their origin, civilization and worship. (1) We know that the Aryans were a white-coloured people; while the Rakshasas are invariably described as a black race. Here, however, the question may be raised that Rama, the hero of the Ramayana, is also described as a black man. This of course is an exceptional case. Besides, as I have elsewhere put it, the author of this popular Epic seems to have had before him an old story of the South which he has grafted upon the story of Rama of Kosala and completed the grand work. the Ramayana. The word Rama itself means "the black one" from the very old Tamilian root ir ( Iṛ ), "to be darkened." [Though the root is now lost, it survives in the following words: இரா (ira), "night"; இருள் (irul) "dark"; இருக்தை (irundai), "charcoal"; இருப்பு (irumbu), "black metal." ( i. e. iron); and இராமன் (Raman), "blackman." The feminine of இராமன் (Raman) is இராமாயி (Ramayi) which we find generally used amomg the lower classes, as proper names.] To the oriental mind, the term 'black' is often associated in idea with beauty. So Raman conveys to the mind the idea of a black but fair man, just as the word காரிணை (Karikai) is suggestive of a "black, but fair woman," from the root கரு (Karu) "to blacken." (2) From the Ramayana we learn that the Rakshasas were a highly civilized people. They had attained a high degree of civilization independently of the Aryans, nay, were even more civilized than the early Aryans. The position assigned to women in the Aryan community was comparatively inferior; among the Rakshasas women held an honourable position. The ancient Dravidian lady was the mistress of the house and heiress and owner of all property, and she held the right to select her husband at her own choice, known as Swayamvaram . But among the Aryans, the marriage system was from very early times Kanyadhanam , "giving of the daughter", and heirship was patriarchal. From the Uttarakanda we learn that Ravana took possession of Lanka by maternal right, for heirship among ancient Dravidians was matriarchal and not as with the Aryan's patriarchal, a clear proof of their different nationality. (See my article on the "Pandavas and the Tamilian Kings", Tamilian Antiquary , No. 1, pp. 61—64). (3) The differences in religion and in worship are also most striking. The Aryans were polytheists and worshippers of heavenly bodies. But the Rakshasas were monotheists and worshippers of Civa, the Supreme Lord of the Dravidas, not included in the Aryan pantheon. Besides, the Aryans were performers of Yágas , while their enemies were destroyers of such bloody sacrifices , which were intended to obtain only some material good. The Aryan worship of natural phenomena and their unmeaning sacrifices appeared to the philosophical Tamil mind to be sacrilegious. The Rakshasas as well as the Asuras of olden days—the ancestors of the Tamilian race,—worshipped their Supreme Lord, the God, Civa, in the form of a Linga, "emblem" or "image" with incense and flowers, and their ultimate aim was the attainment of heavenly bliss. [See my essays on the "Admixture of Aryan with Tamilian," in the pages of the Siddhanta Deepika, and the Educational Review, for years 1900—1901.] These are the most striking differences between the two rival races. They show that they represented two different nationalities and that Ravana and his followers belonged to the Asuras or the ancient Tamilians. And I dare say that Mr. Griffith is right when he says: "The people against whom Rama waged war are different in origin, in civilization, and in worship." Though the name Rakshasa became hated, and contemptible in latter days, it was at first an honorific name and meant “the protectors,” equivalent to the Tamilian word ane or pyane which means “protectors of the country.” Even the proper names in the Epic are sanskritised by the poet as Ravana, Vibheeshana, Kumba-karna, &c. This cannot lead one to treat them as Aryans, for we see also the names of other peoples who were beyond doubt non-Aryan, sanskritised, as Sugriva, Hanuman, Jadayu, &c. Again, it is an acknowledged fact that the Dravidian ethnologically belongs to the Caucasian melanochroid physical type of the human species, a branch of Homo Caucasicus of Mr. Keane. Therefore, there is nothing strange in the remarks of our friend Mr. C.T. Naidu, viz. , “In Lanka some of the Rakshasas were very handsome.” If Monier Williams is of the same opinion as our friend Mr. Tirumalayya Naidu, who quotes him, I should say he is wrong. But the text from his “Indian Wisdom” which I beg to quote below, clearly shows that the Author’s view about the Rakshasas is different from that of Mr. Tirumalayya Naidu. “It is certainly likely,” says M. Williams, “ that at some early date, not long after the first settlement of the Aryan races in the country of the five rivers, rival tribes of immigrants, called Kurus, advancing from that region towards the plains of Hindustan, contended for supremacy. It is, moreover, probable that soon after their first occupation of the Gangetic districts, a body of invaders headed by a bold leader, and aided by the warlike but uncivilized hill-tribes, forced their way southwards unto the Peninsula of India as far as Ceylon. The heroic exploits of the chieftains in both cases would naturally become the theme of epic poetry, and the wild Aborigines of the Vindhya and neighbouring hills would be poetically converted into Monkeys, while the powerful Pre-aryan races of the south would be represented as many-headed ogres and blood-thirsty demons..... In the epic poems they are generally called Rakshasas or evil demons, the relentless enemies of Gods and good men and of all sacred rights.” (Indian Wisdom, p p. 311-313.)

title: The Morality of the Ramayana
author: T. Ponnambalam Pillai
text: The Morality of the Ramayana,* BY Mr. T. PONNAMBALAM PILLAI, M. R. A. S. The late lamented Professor Sundram Pillai of the Trivandram College had, in the course of his extensive study and observation, formed definite opinions on matters connected with his country, but before he was able to give them out to the world, his life was cut short. The following are some of them, known only to a narrow circle of friends. They have been portrayed with Boswellian fidelity in Tamil and published posthumously † by Mr. V. P. Subramanya Moodaliar, one of the Professor's admirers, and himself no mean thinker on social and other allied questions. I have taken the liberty to give to the substance an English garb. It must be stated, at the outset, that the learned Professor had no faith in the authenticity of the story of the Ramayana. He was of opinion that it was meant to proclaim the prowess of the Aryans and represent their rivals and enemies, the Dravidians, who had attained a high degree of civilization at that period, in the worst possible colour. He offers this criticism taking for granted that the story is founded on facts. The country, that lies between the Vindhya mountains and the northern limits of H. H. the Nizam's Dominions, was subject to the rule of Ravana, the King of Ceylon, and his sister Surpanaka was in direct charge of it as his vicerine. * This and the following criticism are reprints from the Malabar Quarterly Review with kind permission. Ed. † Vide Tamilian Antiquary , No. 2. A Critical Review of the Story of the Ramayana, with an introduction by Mr. J. M. Nallasamy Pillai, B.A., B.L., another Dravidian scholar and thinker. The western portion of it was Janasthanam and the eastern portion Dandakaranyam. The whole place was partly inhabited and partly filled with jungles. The country between this tract and the southern limits of Mysore was ruled by the Dravidian kings, Neelan and Vali. The Peninsula further south was the Tamilagam or Tamil country ruled over by the three Tamil kings, Chera, Chola and Pandiya. Special mention is made by Valmiki of the last-mentioned prince. At this period the Aryans were settling themselves down in the unoccupied portions and their colonies were very few and had not extended to the towns. The Sovereigns of these countries as well as of Ceylon were Dravidians or of Dravidian extraction. The high standard of morality set up by them and the perfection attained by them in most of the fine-arts are evident signs of the high civilization reached by them. The masterly account of the metropolis of Ravana and of the golden gate of the Pandian fort as given by Valmiki are more than flights of imagination. Ravana is described as a monster with ten heads and twenty hands, approaching the Grecian Hydra. It has been conclusively proved by Palæontology that animals larger and mightier than elephants were once in existence. But remnants of Rakshasas as those described by Valmiki and his compeers have yet to be found out. It requires no effort to say that the existence of such a class of God's creatures was a myth and the account was made out that the Dravidians might look small in the eyes of posterity. For the same reason the name of Asuras was given to one set of Dravidians. Similarly individuals, belonging to the clan of which Bâli, Sugriva and Hanuman were the leaders, were termed as Monkeys. The Dravidian theory and the existence of the race of ourang-outang have not solved the problem started by the ancient Aryans. The Devas were none but Aryans, opposed to Asuras and Rakshasas. The sages or Munies or Rishis were their priests that accompanied them during their hostile and aggressive march. Ravana, one of the important characters in the Ramayana was versed in the Vedas and was a staunch believer in Civa. The austere penance performed by him was such as to shake even the very foundations of Mount Kailas. His proficiency in music was so great as even to move Civa. He was a renowned warrior and by his personal valour effected great conquests. He administered his kingdom so well that internal peace was never disturbed. He was a dutiful son, father, husband and brother. He could always be relied upon and maintained the laws of war with honour. He treated his enemies with generosity, nay, with magnanimity. The other Dravidian princes, such as Bâli and Neelan, were equally accomplished men and bore the highest character. They administered their kingdoms with characteristic justice and impartiality. The charges against Ravana were:— (1) That he defeated the celestials and imprisoned them, (2) That he annoyed the sages while in the performance of their religious rites. (3) That he abducted Sita, the wife of Rama. As has already been pointed out, the Devas or celestials did not descend from the heavens, but were only the kith and kin of the Aryan trespassers. Their mission was not friendly and they were in quest of conquest. Ravana would therefore have been justified not only in retarding their progress, but also in carrying the campaign into the enemy's country or Deva Loga. He vanished them in a fair fight and there is nothing unusual in imprisoning prisoners of war. With regard to the molestation of the Sages, it has already been stated that they were the Vaidiks or priestly portion of the Aryan intruders. History has repeated itself over and over again. They were the missionaries that preceded the conquest of Dravida by the Aryans. While performing their religious rites or under that cloak they collected and communicated intelligence regarding the movements of the Dravidians to the enemies of the country. As long as they settled themselves down in Dravida, it was their duty to have conformed to its laws and proved loyal to established authority. They not only failed in their duty, but also proved treacherous. Ravana would therefore have been within his rights, to have put them to the sword, but as a pious devotee of Civa he would not take such an extreme step. He contented himself with only molesting them in the performance of their religious rites, fully believing that they would retrace their steps and finally clear out of the country. Under the articles of war there appears nothing unusual in the abduction of Sita. When Ravana, the all-powerful King of Ceylon, heard of the affront offered to his sister—one of the first ladies of the realm—he must naturally have been incensed at the ungallant and cowardly act of the polished brothers. It certainly demanded retribution. It is a right of warfare, to seize and carry away any member of the enemy's party, whether actively engaged in fighting or is found as a straggler. In one of the ancient books of moral precepts, it has been stated that it is the right of a victorious general to carry away the wife of the fallen rival. Ravana went with the object of demanding satisfaction, but in the absence of the brothers, he had a free fight with one of their uncles and his horde and after vanquishing them, carried away Sita. It may be said that Ravana was unfair inasmuch as he caused Lakshmana to be decoyed from the place before he entered the presence of Sita. If he had done so, certainly it must have been unfair. But as the whole incident smacks of supernaturalism, it cannot be accepted. Again, Ravana was in his own dominions, when he heard of the treatment of his sister by Rama and Lakshmana, and he should therefore have advanced towards them with sufficient fighting force. As the insult offered was with impunity, Ravana must naturally have thought that some latent force must have been at the back of the Aryan princes to support them. He should therefore have repaired to the scene with great caution and sufficiently armed. In these circumstances it was unnecessary for him to have allured away Lakshmana. In treating his prisoner he was very considerate. When Sita was first seized he would not permit any body to touch her person, but caused her to be carried with her seat(?). Hi; further behaviour towards the Princess shows his magnanimity. When she was taken to Lanka she was housed in one of the most beautiful palaces situated in his ornamental garden where he used to repair for health and recreation. Her attendants were the select princesses from the royal family. Though he was passionately in love with Sita he only made overtures directly or indirectly and never thought of using brute force as it was quite in his power to do so. Owing to the conduct of her husband and brother-in-law there were occasions when Ravana could have put her to death, particularly after learning that she would not yield to his wishes for anything under the sun, but his generosity and piety would not permit him to do anything of the kind. What did the polished Aryan princes do in a similar situation? At the instance of Visvamitra, Rama killed Tadaka, the grand-mother of Ravana, for annoying the priestly class. Again when his sister made love to the brothers passing no doubt all bounds of modesty (if the Aryan Chronicler is to be believed) they not only insulted her, but mutilated her features. This was no act of gallantry and Rama looked at the whole thing with an unconcerned eye, without raising one word of disapproval at the conduct of his brother. Again according to the code of international law there was no declaration of war to warrant such a barbarity which is not heard of even in the crudest of ages.
