Rama and his brother were the most polished gentlemen of the age and it is an enigma how they perpetrated such an act of cruelty towards a helpless woman. This is in perfect contrast to the manner in which the so-called monster king behaved himself. Next to the offences committed by Bâli. As has already been pointed out he was the ruling prince of the country south of Dandakaranyam and the fact was so by right of primogeniture. During a temporary absence from his kingdom, on a pursuit of conquest he left his brother Sugriva in charge of it, as his regent, but on his return he found his unnatural brother ambitious of becoming the King himself and proved refractory by refusing to hand over the reins of Government. Bali had to fight for regaining his Kingdom. The result was the defeat and exile of his brother Sugriva. In a similar situation any other person, take for example Aurangazib, would have made an end of his brother that he might not give trouble again. But his brotherly feeling prevailed upon him to spare his life. The Aryans have found fault with Bâli for all this, but no reasonable man will do so on the facts stated. It has also been alleged that Bâli took his brother's wife for himself. Even if the authority of the Aryan Chronicler is to be relied upon, the code of warfare permitted such an act on the part of a victorious enemy as has already been stated. But the partisan account has to be taken with caution. The Professor and his friend appear to think that Bâli was generous enough not to molest the household of his erring brother and they chose to remain where they were without following Sugriva in his exile. It is also possible that the members of the family were detained as hostages for his good behaviour. Before concluding this paper some reference may be made to some minor facts. The Professor and his friend are loud in their condemnation of the alliances formed between Rama and Sugriva, and Rama and Vibheeshana as unnatural and unbecoming of dignified, straight-forward and gallant Kshatriyas. Here I would draw the special attention of the reader to the part played by Rama during the last and fatal battle that was fought between Bali and Sugriva. While it was raging, from his place of concealment Rama shot Bâli dead. It is unnecessary to repeat that this cowardly conduct is not becoming a Kshatriya. There are stories of Kshatriyas wounded on the back, committing suicide ashamed of meeting their spouses in that condition, as it was considered that only cowards receive such wounds and not heroes who fight face to face. In that light the act of Rama was mean in the extreme and his only object was to secure an alliance at any cost. Vibheeshana was a great coward in as much as he never took part in any of the battles that were fought between his brother's forces and those of Rama. His services were required by the latter only to ascertain the weak points of his enemy. In other words Rama relied more upon subterfuges than fair open fight which was the Dharma of the Kshatriyas according to Aryan ideas. Now I have only to submit that in stating these facts the authority of Valmiki alone was relied upon and none else.

title: The Morality of the Ramayana: a Review
author: T. Sadasiva Aiyar
text: “The Morality of the Ramayana” A Review. BY Mr. T. SADASIVA AIYER, B. A., M. L. When I read the article on the above subject by my friend, Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai, in the last issue of the Malabar Quarterly Review , an article to which the Editor was pleased to give the leading place in the Magazine, I rubbed my eyes to see that I was not dreaming. I know that the late lamented Mr. Sundaram Pillai, whom I and numerous others used to admire at a distance, had some queer notions about the uselessness of the Sanskrit Vedas, the utter unimportance of intonations in the pronunciation of Mantras, and about the character and signification of Monkeys and Rakshasas in the Ramayana. But even he seemed to have been unwilling or ashamed to publish the crude ideas about the morality of the Ramayana which have now been resuscitated from his manuscripts by Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai and others; or perhaps the learned professor had become doubtful in his ripe manhood of the validity of his criticisms and the utility of publishing them. Those who, like myself, cherish his memory with affection and admiration as a Tamil scholar and antiquarian, a thinker of great originality and a facile wielder of the English tongue, cannot but be pained at this unnecessary publication of his views about the Ramayana after his death. I am not going to refute the logic and the conclusions of the article. Professor Sundaram Pillai was, I admit, a great and good man, and my friend, Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai, is, no doubt, a worthy disciple of the deceased scholar. But their greatness when compared with Sree Ramachandra's is as a farthing rush-light to the Sun in his mid-day glory, and their opinions of Sree Rama cannot, of course, affect Sree Rama, who must, no doubt, be greatly amused by His children's prattle about Him. He may be even right glad that some of His children remember and pronounce His Holy Name even if they raise their voices against that name in puny anger and irritation. Valmiki's and Thulasi Das' and Kamban's Ramayanams will not cease to be read and admired by countless future generation to their moral and spiritual benefit as their works have been read in the past; Kabir Das and Ram Das are not going to lose their places in the list of God's Holy Saints; our people from Maharajas down to the humblest menial classes are not going to publish in the next Gazette that they have changed their names from Rama Varma, Ram Chunder Gose, Rama Prasad, Rama Iyer, or Rama Pulaya to Ravana Prasad, Ravana Iyer, etc., the Malayalis are not going to substitute the reading of "Milestones from Tamil History" for the reading of Ezhuthacchan's Ramayana at their Sambandham ceremonies, and the Northern Hindus are not going to drop the national greeting of "Ram, Ram," when they meet each other, and the Ramkrishna Mission is not going to call itself the Rakshasa Kamsa Mission; and people are not going to discard Rama-Nama as a Tharaka Manthram; none of those things is going to happen owing to the attacks of Professor Sundaram Pillai and Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai on the morality of the Ramayana and owing to the unmanly cowardice and treachery of Sree Rama conclusively proved by their logic. In our younger and wilder days, most of us were inclined to atheism and we took delight in tilting at sacred things and we were incapable of exalting or appreciating one thing without depreciating another. I used in my younger and more foolish days to abuse Sree Krishna and to make fun of His taking birth in a dirty human womb whenever I met a Vaishnava and whenever I wanted to exalt Lord Mahadeva. I have no doubt that I felt at those times greater pleasure in wounding the Vaishnava's feeling than in exalting Lord Mahadeva. But when we have passed a certain age, especially the age of fifty according to our Shastras, or of the age of fifty-five according to the Civil Service Regulation, we are expected to get rid of these puerile and useless vanities and to speak and write only words useful to the world and not those which can lead only to disunion and strife. As I said above, I am not going to criticise Mr. Ponnambalam's article in detail. Controversies used to be carried on several years ago in the vernacular between the very learned Somasundara Naicker of Chulai and Sree Srinivasa Sastrial of the Brahma Vidya Press and hard hits used to be given on both sides. Both together used sometimes to join forces to attack their common enemy viz., the Vaishnavas. Such controversies in the vernacular carried on by intellectual giants used to give huge delight to us, lesser mortals, in our younger days, and, as everybody knew that those learned men were fanatics in some respects (both of them, I believe became quite mellowed in spiritual wisdom and became fully tolerant in their last days,) and, as everybody knew that it was a hallowed tradition of vernacular controversies for each side to call the other a fool or a rogue and even to abuse each other's ancestors and relations and to dub the other side's God a fraud so as to add hot condiments and sauce to the dry polemics, readers of such vernacular controversies allowed the usual large discount and took the very valuable and spiritual learning spread out by both sides without their mental digestion being spoiled by the hot fanaticism displayed. But Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai has introduced the same method of controversy in an English article and the Editor has thought it fit to give it a prominent place. May I ask the Editor whether, instead of the Valmiki Ramayanam and Sree Ramachandra's character having been attacked, Lord Jesus or Lord Mahomet, or the Bible or the Koran, had been attacked in an article contributed by one who despised those Great Beings or works, would the Editor have allowed it to appear in his magazine as readily as he (a Hindu) has allowed Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai's resuscitation of Professor Sundaram Pillai's attack on Sree Rama and the Ramayana even without an editorial note or explanation?* The Editor may be an agnostic or unitarian theist, and yet he would have hesitated before publishing a virulent attack on a Being and work held in religious reverence by millions of his brother men. I shall only add in concluding this portion of my letter that I am unable to see in what parts of Valmiki's Ramayanam he found the following statements referred to in his article. Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai says that in stating his "facts the authority of Valmiki alone was relied upon, and none else;" a. Ravana "was a dutiful son...husband...brother." "He treated his enemies with generosity," b. "Ravana went with the object of demanding satisfaction, but in the absence of the brothers he had a fierce fight with one of their uncles and his horde" (as if Jatayu fought assisted by a horde) "and after vanquishing them carried away Sita." * [It is not clear what Mr. T. Sadasiva Aiyar is objecting to. Is it the publication of the article the Morality of the Ramayana , in the Review or publishing it in a prominent place or publishing it without an editorial note or explanation? If he thinks that the Editor should have exercised his censorship and refrained from giving publication to such an article, we fear he has completely misunderstood our attitude, which is purely neutral and non-partisan, in an historical controversy of the kind proposed by Mr. T. Ponnambalam Pillai and into which the present writer wants to import the flavour of theological implications. Whoever has known the late Professor Sundaram Pillai and Mr. T. Ponnambalam Pillai has known them as persons who would be the last to wantonly wound the religious susceptibilities of the people. As for ourselves, the very fact that we have published this refutation as readily as we published the original article should be sufficient to show that we are trying, in our own way, to hold the balance even between the opposing views of the Pro-Aryan and Pro-Dravidian scholars. The saying of Aristotle "Socrates is dear to me, Plato is dear to me, but Truth is dearer than all these" must particularly be borne in mind in this connection. About publishing the article as the first in the number, it is scarcely necessary to point out that a journal is not like a lecture-hall where the front seats are reserved for the bigwigs while the common herd is relegated to the back benches and that various are the considerations which weigh with the Editor in determining, or it may be, in not determining, the place of an article in each issue of his journal, and which, we think, need not be detailed out here. Coming to our omission to add an explanatory foot-note, we doubt whether ninty per cent of our contributors would not take such editorial activity amiss and whether from the stand-point of the writers primarily it would not be generally preferable to leave their productions to speak for themselves instead of tagging on to them our individual views. This general consideration apart, there is further the special one that few Editors would or could undertake to have a body of cut and dried opinions on all the conceivable subjects dealt with in their journal.—ED. M. Q. R.] c. "Thataka" was the grand-mother of Ravana." d. Sugriva was ambitious of becoming the king himself and proved refractory by refusing to hand over the reins of Government; and Vali had to fight for regaining his kingdom. e. Vibheeshana was a great coward inasmuch as he never took part in any of the battles that were fought between his brother's forces and those of Rama. f. The country that lies between the Vindhya Mountains and the northern limits of His Highness the Nizam's dominions was subject to the rule of Ravana." Every one of those statements is directly opposed to Valmiki's version. The very first Sloka in the 5th Chapter of the Bala Kandam of the Ramayanam says that the entire land of India belonged to the Solar line of Kings; and that is also what Sree Rama tells Vali in justification of Vali's punishment as a subject of the Solar Kings and not as an independent chief. Vibheeshana fought strenuously and bravely in Rama's cause and was taunted by Indrajith for so doing and was saved from Ravana's Sakthi (directed against him) by the intervention of Sree Lakshmana. Sugriva did not want to become King, but was pressed by the people to become King, and as soon as Vali came back, surrendered the kingdom and explained matters humbly, and Vali had not at all to fight to regain his kingdom. Thataka was the mother of Mareecha, and she was a Gandharva woman who lost that form through her sin. Ravana was afraid of Sree Rama and Lakshmana and went like a thief to abduct Sita and killed the poor old Jatayu who tried to prevent him. Ravana disobeyed his father's wishes, insulted his brother Kubera and deprived him of his Pushpaka Vimanam; killed his brother's messenger, abducted by force virtuous ladies against the remonstrauces of his wife Mandodari. But why should I insult the intelligence of your Hindu readers by contradicting in detail all the wild statements made in the article as if they were taken from Valmiki's Ramayanam? If Professor Sundram Pillai does not believe in the Ramayanam story at all, as Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai begins by saying in the second para of his article, why should he attack the Aryans on the basis of the allegations in that story after distorting the allegation for his purpose? And if you attack a character as disclosed in a story, is it at all fair or charitable to take certain facts alone as stated in that story as true, to take other statements, which qualify or explain those facts, as false, and then build up a theory? In a very early Chapter (5th) of the very first Kandam of the Ramayana the author Valmiki begins by stating that the Ikshwaku race owned the whole of the land surrounded by seas, and the very name of Dandakaranyam shows (see also the Uttara Ramayanam) its connection with one of the kings of the Solar race. And yet we are gravely told that Sree Rama invaded the Dandakaranya and the Janasthana which belonged to Ravana. Surpanaka, it is said, was a quite innocent and harmless lady and was doing nothing out of the way when her ears were cut off. But Valmiki says that she sprang on Sita and tried to eat her up, as she thought that the only obstacle to Sree Rama's becoming her (Surpanaka's) husband was the existence alive of Sita. (Chapter XVIII, Aranya Kandam). Of course, Valmiki is a liar when he says this, and Professor Sundaram Pillai and Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai have been able to separate this lie from the truthful portions of the narrative, which portions show these learned gentlemen what rascals these Aryans were and what glorious and virtuous people the Rakshasas as a class were with the exception of Vibheeshana and his four ministers. These latter did fight with weapons on Rama's side according to Valmiki. The monkeys who fought on Rama's side were not ordinary monkeys but hybrids born to Devas. Of course all these statements of Valmiki are puerile, worthless, or cunning additions according to Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai, and these monkeys were really Tamil Dravidians. So also, if Vali himself admitted to Sree Ramachandra that he was rightly punished by the Ruling Power at Ayodhya through Sree Rama's hands (see Chapter XVIII, Kishkindha Kandam), this is also a lying trick of Valmiki. This author is a great fool as well as a great liar according to those who do not believe in Higher Being, Higher Worlds and Subtler Forces and Siddhis than obtain among ordinary men and in the physical world. He seems to admit that prima fucie Lord Sree Rama's action required justification, but if he was an imaginative liar, why should he not say that Vali was killed in open fight? The Sūkshma Dharma in Valivadham lies, no doubt, very deep. Of course, it is easy to flippantly and conceitedly say that Sree Rama was a wretched selfish man like us and that this is a sufficient explanation for his act. That Vali had warnings from his wife Thara, that Sree Rama was going to deal with Vali's crimes as a King's Officer to a criminal and not as a foe against an independent foe, and that she tried to persuade him to get forgiveness from Sree Rama and thus escape punishment, are told clearly in the Valmiki's Ramayana. We must however be thankful for even small mercies at the hands of these scholars, for they seem not to have attacked the honesty and character of that wretched fool and traitor, Hanuman, who, though a Dravidian, is the head of the Bhakthas of Sree Ramachandra. I know that there are some who think that all my Indian brothers who are now nominally classed as Sudras, though most of them are Vaisyas and some of them ought to be classed as Kshathriyas and Brahmins,—but that is another story—do not belong to the Aryan race. It is not improbable that the Vellala and Naga races were originally races not belonging to the Fifth Arya race, but to a later branch of the later Fourth Turanian Race, that branch being called Dravidians. The Fifth Arya Race itself was selected out of the flower of the earlier Fourth Race. But the Aryan race itself had developed all the four castes long before Sree Rama's days. At first, there was only one caste, and then three castes arose, and lastly four castes. The Sudras of the United Provinces and Bombay cannot be said to be Dravidians. Vellalas, or Nagas. Many conquered and indigenous races belonging to an earlier civilization must, of course, have also been taken into the Aryan Caste system afterwards. Some of the more enlightened and religious members belonging to such indigenous races were incorporated, as even Kshathriyas and Vysias. But the ambition of many of my Southern Vellala friends and of the so-called non-Brahmin portion of our community in the southern portions of India to now cut themselves entirely adrift from Sree Rama and Sree Krishna and the Sanskrit Vedas and the Thiruvaimozhi Prabandham and to rise a standard of revolt on a pure Tamil Saivite anti-Brahmin and non-Aryan basis, is, if I may be permitted to say so, an utter wildgoose chase. I do not mean, of course, to say that the Saiva Siddhantha Religion of Philosophical Devotion so splendidly expounded by my brother J. M. Nallasamy Pillai, which is the same as the religion of the Gita with slight variations of terminology, is at all opposed to the Arya Vedas and Shasthras. The non-Brahmin Alwars who have been devotees of Sree Rama and Sree Krishna are infinitely more powerful than my modern Tamil friends of the type of Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai, intellectual giants of vast learning, though many of these latter may be. We have already got strife and division enough among us. A new religious sect based not on the enunciation of a new spiritual truth but on critical attack of the Ramayana and of Sree Rama's character need not be set up to cause further strife and dissension among us. The political, anti-quarian, and religious importance of the Vellala community and the great beauty and spirituality of the Tamil Sacred Literature need not be founded on attacks upon the Ramayana and the morality of the Aryan races, to which most so-called Sudras belong either wholly as in the north or by a large infusion of Aryan blood as in Malabar, and we know how in the political field the assertion of superiority in political status and loyalty and character by a section of Indians is embarassing and delaying the introduction of Lord Morley's Reforms. Fanaticism and extremism in political, social, and religious matters though better than death and apathy, are not at all desirable things in themselves, and as it seemed to me to be the duty of every sober critic to try his best to put down the rising flames raised in these fields in respectable Journals and Magazines before the flames spread havoc and as soon they have done their work of giving warmth and life to chilled and numbed limbs, I have ventured to write this imperfect protest during the few snatches of leisure I am able to secure, against the implications contained in the article of my friend Mr. Ponnambalam Pillai, whose hand has been probably utilised half-unconsciously to himself by a mischievous Spirit from another world bent on showing discord and disunion among us. When I refer to the Ramayana of Valmiki as a Spiritual Work and also as a Historical narrative, I, of course, do not intend to state that the work (every word and letter of it) has come down to us as it was first expressed to his disciples, Bharadwaja and others, by the great Sage. As a reviewer in the Hindu of 20th July last put it: “notwithstanding the ravages of time, it has come down to us with” (practically) “unsullied purity, though interpolations of a marked character are inevitable in a work so huge and stupendous in character ,” But to first state the whole thing to be a fiction, then to select garbled and isolated passages and incidents as if they alone were genuine and showed the morality and spirituality of the Author’s work and of the hero of the work, instead of taking the pervading and clearly recognisable trend and spirit of the whole, are, I must repeat, grossly unfair and show a mind diseased by ‘inveterate and’ bigoted prejudice against the very name “Aryan.”

title: The Morality of the Ramayana: a Rejoinder
author: T. Ponnambalam Pillai
text: The Morality of the Ramayana—A Rejoinder. BY MR. T. PONNAMBALAM PILLAI, M. R. A. S. In preparing my paper on the Morality of Ramayana , to the “Malabar Quarterly Review” I intended to interpret the views of the late professor Sundaram Pillai, to a larger circle of readers than the Tamil article, in the Tamilian Antiquary , (No. 2), was able to command, in order to elicit rational criticism, in the interests of the Southern Indian History. As education advances it is but natural that investigations into the history of one’s own land, particularly if it is enveloped in mystery, should be made. At all events, such a spirit pervades at present the minds of all educated men both in Southern India and Ceylon, where most of the scenes in the Ramayana have been laid. If in the course of such a legitimate enquiry old ideas are exploded, all right thinking people ought to welcome such a healthy change, and sympathise with the workers in their difficult labours. In the place of such generous treatment, I least expected a furious, but a pointless attack, from the pen of Mr. Sadasiva Iyer, the talented Chief Justice of Travancore, who is known for his perfect equanimity of temper, and who until now never permitted it to be ruffled by anything, as became an arbiter of Justice in the Highest Court of the kingdom. I also regret, that in the heat of the fight he should have so forgotten himself, as to introduce into the arena of discussion, a large number of unparliamentary expressions (about 40 in number besides unlimited inuendoes), thus following the vernacular controversies he has condemned after taking exception to my using certain strong terms; and as a crowning act, that he should have suggested, that some evil spirit, probably from the nether world, impelled me to set my pen to the article in question. What I regret more than anything, is his reference to my motives, and the introduction of politics into the review of my paper. In the first place, it is hard that I should be denounced, as attacking a class, if in the course of making a statement of certain historical facts, it is placed in an unfavourable light. In the next place, it was in no light-heartedmood, or with the object of ridiculing the worship of Rama, that I penned the article which Mr. Sadasiva Iyer criticises. I should perhaps have added the warning with which Mr. V.P. Subramania Mudaliar, the author of the Tamil version prefaced it, viz. that it was only an historical aspect of the question. It is however gratifying to me that my reviewer credits me with the Saiva Siddhantha faith. The broad and cosmopolitan principles which it inculcates are embodied in the following stanza of the Kunda-Purana (கக்ஷ காண்டய, கந்தவிரதப்படலம்.) எவ்வெவார் தம்மையேனும் யாவரே பெனினும் போற்றின், அவ்வவரிடமாக் விசாண்டே, யவர்க்கருள் தருவாய் போற்றி, மெய்வரு தெளிவிலுண்ணை வெளிப்படவுணர்ந்துள் ளோர்க்குத், தெய்வத போக முத்தி சிறப்பொடு தருவாய் போற்றி.” “ Whosoever may worship Thee in whatsoever aspect, Thou wilt present Thyself as such, and grant him grace. To those that understand Thee aright, Thou wouldst grant beatitude gracefully. I adore such a Deity.” If I adhere to these views (and I assure my readers that I do) I cannot consistently trifle with the faith inculcated in the Ramayana, and will not directly, or indirectly, consciously or unconsciously, indulge in such a treatment as that with which I have been fathered by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer; though it is a difficult thing to question the absurdities and supernaturalisms that have been smuggled into it by some of its deluded votaries. To construct a reliable history of Southern India constant reference has to be made to the Ramayana, one of the few sources of ancient record. But dealing, as it does, with hoary antiquity, garbed as the facts are in our inherent national hyperbole, drawn as the imageries are in such a way as to border upon mythology, and unrestrained as the chroniclers are in their indulgence to the fullest extent, in the license which poetry permits, it should be the endeavour of every sane man to allow the facts to be treated as historical truths, to be put to a crucial scientific test. It is my humble, but my firm belief, that this test consists in courting healthy and open criticism of all doubtful facts. This is an experience. not at all foreign to my critic, who had large experience as a Judicial Officer. In performing this task, if I am charged with the offence of disturbing the established faith, my reply is that the end justifies the means. Now as to politics. I repeat that I regret the introduction of this subject into the discussion. I have always had a natural disinclination to discuss it, and the unfortunate condition of India at the present moment makes any reference to the topic unsavory. If I am compelled to enter the lists, Mr. Sadasiva Aiyar alone is responsible for my doing so. In the course of his criticism, he says that the delay in the introduction of Lord Morley's reforms is due to the conduct of people like my humble self. But as is evident from the published reports, it is due to that generous spirit which prompted the benign British Government to launch the whole scheme. Here I must digress for a moment to explain myself and to enable Mr. Sadasiva Aiyar to refresh his memory in the study of ancient history.* ..... I think I should make one more preliminary observation, before proceeding to the discussion of the main subject, in order to correct what I may term, a historical solecism. Mr. Sadasiva Iyer speaks in a patronising tone saying that certain Dravidian friends of his, ought to be counted as Brahmins and Kshatrias and I believe if he had the power he would have raised them to that dignity. He further adds that there is a large infusion of Aryan blood amongst the Dravidians, but failed to state the reverse. It has * [We have omitted the paragraphs which follow this, as the policy of our journal prohibits publishing discussions of this kind. Ed.] already been pointed out,* that when the Aryans entered Northern India, they did so as conquerors and not as peaceful emigrants, though at a later stage they became identified with the races already in possession of the land. But it was the other way when they entered Southern India, and they were enabled to do so only by the sufferance of the Dravidians. I make this statement on the authority of the Ramayana itself. During his exile, when Rama travelled from place to place he took care to ascertain, where to get lodgings for himself and his two relations from friendly people, and how to protect themselves from man and beast ( vide canto 54 Ayodyakanda). Again the fact that Agastia, the sage, was constantly subject to attacks from such individuals, as Sutha, the husband of Tadaka, Tadaka herself, and her son Mareecha (canto 25, Balakanda), that the sages at Chitrakuta had to abandon their dwellings owing to the ill-treatment of Kara of Janasthana, that Rama was able only to hear their complaints and sympathise with them (canto 116, Ayodyakanda) and that he had clandestinely to make an alliance with Sugriva at the Rishyamuka Ranges, while Vali more powerful than Ravana was holding undisputed sway over Kishkintha (canto 10, Kishkinthakanda), go to show that that the Aryans were dependent upon the pleasure of, and seekers of favour from, the permanent dwellers of the soil. In these circumstances, they would only have been too glad to enter into close relationship with the all-powerful natives. Mr. Sadasiva Iyer makes a serious admission. For he says “that many conquered and indigenous races belonging to an earlier civilization must of course have been taken into Aryan caste system. Some of the more enlightened and religious members belonging to such indigenous races, were incorporated as even Kshatrias and Vysias”; and I ask why not as Brahmins? The statement made by Mr. Sadasiva Iyer is an historical truth, as the result of the evolution of the society, when * See pages 47-50 of the Malabar Quarterly Review , Vol. IX. No. 1 March, 1910. an emigrant people mix with a resident population. It has been authoritatively established, that the Dravidians were not the indigenous races of Southern India. They belong to an earlier wave of emigration, and in all probability, the first batch of them crossed over by sea from Western Asia, as is evident from their skill as sailors. Notwithstanding the nick-names of giants and monkeys given to them by the Aryans, the description given in the Ramayana of their cities and buildings, the high standard of morality observed by the generality of them, and the state of efficiency and discipline in which their armies were maintained, go to show the high level of civilization attained by them. This was their condition when the Aryans crossed the Indus ( vide Vedic India Page 291). After centuries when they advanced towards the south, though there were the usuai bickerings in the beginning, both the races became reconciled to each other, and identified with one another, so as to form a single nation. From what has fallen from Kiplar, a poet of the last Academy at Madura, it seems that the caste system was introduced into Southern India at a late stage.
